body:
I agree that the global proportion of Safari 10.1 users is rather small. However, it may vary significantly for different projects. E.g. if some website is targeting vintage mac owners, it's easy to imagine that this proportion will be way-way more.

I have a project where the proportion of IE11 users is crazy, but that's because the content mainly targets a certain economic group. People are on old Windows machines, which explains the numbers.

If someone is developing a website and is new to Next.js, how do they start? They look at the list of supported browsers, see that it's IE11 or greater, get happy and proceed to `next dev`. If Safari module fixing is off by default, the browser range in README would have to contain a disclaimer, explaining some odd caveat that applies to some specific Safari version. The developer will be like: _Is Safari 10.1 the latest? Or is it not? I'd rather check. Oh, it's not so much prevalent, but who knows maybe my users will come from this browser often (my website will be BIG). I'd probably rather turn that thing on, just in case. How do I do this? Oh, here is this other section of the docs about the config, hmmm. How does this even work? StackOverflow, HALP!_ At least 30 minutes are lost even before the first page was written. And this scenario will be quite likely for someone starting their first Next.js project.

Alternative scenario: A team ships a website, it becomes successful, but then they start getting some odd user feedback from a small proportion of customers and go investigating. Half a day is lost + the website did not 'sell' stuff for hundreds of people already.

Now what will happen if Safari fix is on by default? Bundle size will increase by 312 bytes (ungzipped) for everyone, plus there will exist a small script event listener. Both seem nothing in the scale of the entire web app. How can I as a developer 'lose time'? Perhaps, only if I go to the app's generated HTML page source, read it carefully, notice some odd code block and become curious about what it does. I search for it, come across the option and turn it off to save a few bytes of my app size. What proportion of developers will go down this road? My guess that this number will be comparable with the one for global Safari 10.1 users 😀
This seems correct to handle the non-transpiled class methods

body:
Specifying "modern targets" doesn't make much sense IMO. Targeting `esmodules` _is_ the target, which means a very specific set of browser versions:
https://github.com/babel/babel/blob/master/packages/babel-preset-env/data/built-in-modules.json

If the user wanted to target even newer features, IMO they should use a single-bundle built targeting their preferred modern versions.

Is there value in saying "I want IE 11 support and last 2 versions of evergreen only"? That leaves a massive user gap.

Further bundle size optimization like this is blocked on a `srcset` attribute or similar for `<script>` IMO.

This plugin appears to be very fragile and tightly integrated into webpack's internals.

It seems to be simulating a third compiler, e.g. [re-running all provided plugins](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/7704/files#diff-c8386495c7607bdb08870b52e32c7e87R199) and [re-computing the chunk graph](https://github.com/zeit/next.js/pull/7704/files#diff-c8386495c7607bdb08870b52e32c7e87R230).

If my understanding is correct, it's also re-babeling the individual files rather than chunks as a whole (effectively rebundling instead of post-processing emitted chunks).

The only way I feel we could justify this plugin is if it post-processed already computed chunks, however, that comes with its own problems like skipping the webpack plugin flow for user customizations (e.g. service worker, etc).

What's the real value we're deriving from this? It seems to me we're rather instantiate a third webpack instance. This would greatly simplify the implementation and delete the need for this plugin.

----

If the upside to this plugin is to save "rework" within `node_modules`, I'd argue that point is moot. AFAIK the ecosystem is wanting to move to a place where all npm modules are published in ES.Latest, meaning `node_modules` will need to be compiled (and then re-compiled for the modern bundle).

Please let me know if I've misunderstood something!

This is needed to preload `type=module` scripts. We need to set a crossOrigin attribute in this case because[ `<script type="module">` with no crossorigin attribute indicates a credentials mode of `omit`](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2017/12/modulepreload).


So I need to set a value to make sure the that cache value matches

Yes, so the plugin is spawning a new child compiler and rebuilding the files with a different babel  config.

The biggest advantage of this approach is the build times. I documented the build times with this plugin added to a few production sites

Website | Build time - before | Build time - after
-- | -- | --
Hello World | ~2.2s | ~2.7s
Material-UI internal website | ~6s | ~7s
geo.data.gouv.fr/en | ~9s | ~13s

I also tried this for a few more sites, i will try to get those times aw well. So the biggest advantage here is that the build times don't double. 

I also experimented with the other approaches you mentioned before deciding on this one. 
With a third webpack instance the build times were doubling. 
With the post-processing approach, like you mentioned we skip the webpack bundling and plugin flow, so this needed a sort of workaround to include babelHelpers and polyfills. I stopped investigating this when I did not see much build time improvements.

I feel like this is a hybrid approach where we get a new compilation instance, in which we can target modern specific optimizations, and we don't end up dowbling build times due to webpack's internal cache. 

> If the upside to this plugin is to save "rework" within node_modules

I don't think this is an upside we considered. At the moment we avoid compiling `node_modules`, but in the future we want to do that.

Let me know if I was able to answer your concerns

body: Moved this behavior to the plugin.

At this point we already know we're in modern-mode, does the `noModule` property within `script` even matter anymore?

This is client-side code already being executed that was loaded via the `type=module` directive.

```suggestion
    if (process.env.__NEXT_MODERN_BUILD) {
```

`process.env.__NEXT_MODERN_BUILD` is used to enable disable feature during build time
`'noModule' in script` tells us if the current browser supports `type=module`

OK, but the above code always returns the modern bundle if the feature is on then, regardless of `'noModule' in script`:
```js
  static getScriptRoute (route) {
    const scriptName = route === '/' ? '/index' : route
    return `${scriptName}${process.env.__NEXT_MODERN_BUILD ? '.module' : ''}.js`
  }
```

This means ☝️ this code needs to also check `noModule`, or the `__NEXT_MODERN_BUILD` needs to alternate `true`/`false`.
My first comment assumed the alternating was taking place.

This behavior makes it preload *only modern chunks* if the feature is turned on.

Ditto for the others.

Is that what we want?
I guess it makes sense since `<link rel="preload" />` is a newer browser feature — I'm just double checking.

Maybe we want to user-agent sniff this?

We decided to preload only modern when the feature is enabled for now. User agent sniffing is something we want to look into, but right now that means the server responses can't be cached or should include the UA string as part of the cache?
I mainly wanted to move the feature detection into a function because it gets really messy adding it to each statement. Maybe I can call it `formatPath` instead?
